articles.title: Naga Ancestral Remains Return Home from the Pitt Rivers Museum: Revisiting a Colonial History
articles.description: Colonel Prakash Bhatt (Retd)The return of Naga ancestral remains from the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford marks an important moment in the history of the Naga people. It is not merely a matter of returning objects held in a museum collection; it is about restoring ancestors to their homeland, acknowledging historical injustices, and recognising the dignity and cultural significance of human remains. In 2020, the Pitt Rivers Museum closed temporarily due to the COVID-19 pandemic. During this period, a decision was taken to remove displays of shrunken heads and other human remains that had been exhibited since the 1940s, as part of the Museum's decolonisation efforts. This decision, together with the Museum's wider commitment to change, opened the door to conversations that had previously not been possible. Since then, the Museum has worked collaboratively with Naga partners, particularly the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR), and other organisations across the Naga homeland to determine how their ancestors should be returned. The Pitt Rivers Museum and Its Colonial CollectionsThe Pitt Rivers Museum houses the archaeological and anthropological collections of the University of Oxford. Founded in 1884, it began with a donation of approximately 22,000 objects by Lieutenant General Augustus Pitt Rivers. Born Augustus Henry Lane-Fox in 1827, he inherited a 27,000-acre estate in Dorset from his great-uncle in 1880, along with the Pitt Rivers family name. Over the years, the Museum's collections expanded to more than 600,000 items, including significant photographic holdings. A substantial part of these collections was donated by colonial officials, travellers, scholars, and missionaries. Pitt Rivers began his military career at Sandhurst and developed an early interest in the historical development and improvement of weapons. He was an ardent supporter of the emerging anthropological theory of evolution and believed that the progression of human society could be illustrated through the development of weapons, from the spear to the rifle. Collecting artefacts became his passion, and by the end of his life his personal collection had grown to more than 22,000 objects. However, it was not simply his enthusiasm for collecting that earned him the title of the 'Father of British Archaeology', but also his distinctive approach to the classification of artefacts. The institution that bears his name subsequently became an important repository of material collected from different parts of the world, including India's Northeast. Hutton, Mills and the Collection of Naga Ancestral RemainsMost of the Naga ancestral remains now held in the Pitt Rivers Museum's collection were taken to Oxford by John Henry Hutton and James Philip Mills, both administrators and anthropologists who served in the Naga Hills during the British colonial period, approximately between 1910 and 1940. John Henry Hutton (27 June 1885–23 May 1968) served as Deputy Commissioner of Naga Hills District from 1917 to 1935, while James Philip Mills (1890–1960) served in the same position from 1935 to 1937. Hutton was the son of a Church of England clergyman and served as an anthropologist and administrator in the Indian Civil Service (ICS). His years of service in Assam generated a deep interest in the tribal cultures of the region, which became central to his academic work. Joining the ICS in 1909, Hutton spent most of his career in Assam. His responsibilities as a Political Officer and Deputy Commissioner involved extensive tours across the region to inspect facilities and infrastructure and settle legal disputes. In 1920, he was additionally appointed Honorary Director of Ethnography for Assam. His anthropological research was encouraged by Henry Balfour, the first Curator of the Pitt Rivers Museum, who in 1922 visited Hutton in the Naga Hills. Hutton published several important works on the tribal cultures of the region, including The Angami Nagas and The Sema Nagas. His research earned him a Doctor of Science degree from the University of Oxford in 1921. He resigned from the Indian Civil Service in 1936 for family reasons and possibly also to devote more time to research. James Philip Mills (1890–1960) was another prominent member of the Indian Civil Service and an ethnographer. He joined the ICS in 1913 and was posted to Assam Province. In 1916, he was assigned to the Naga Hills District, where he served as Subdivisional Officer based at Mokokchung and later became Deputy Commissioner of the Naga Hills District, based at Kohima, during the 1930s. During his time at Oxford, Mills developed an interest in anthropology and was inspired by Henry Balfour, the Curator of the Pitt Rivers Museum. Together with his colleague J.H. Hutton, he made significant ethnographic collections for the institution. Mills also published three monographs on the Nagas: The Lhota Nagas (1922), The Ao Nagas (1926), and The Rengma Nagas (1937). In 1930, he was appointed Honorary Director of Ethnography for Assam. From 1943 to 1947, he served as Adviser to the Governor of Assam for Tribal Areas and States. Collecting, Colonial Power and the Pangsha ExpeditionIt is important to recognise that colonial 'collecting' was not necessarily the neutral, scholarly activity that the term might suggest. As Arkotong Longkumer, Dolly Kikon, and Laura Van Broekhoven argue in their forthcoming chapter, Repatriation: Slowing, Caring and Witnessing: Naga Human Remains and the Work of Time, collecting was frequently intertwined with structures of colonial violence. Human remains and cultural objects were often confiscated during punitive military expeditions rather than freely given. James Philip Mills provides an account of such activities during the Pangsha Expedition of 1936. He describes undertaking an expedition to Pangsha village, primarily at the request of neighbouring Naga communities who were reportedly being terrorised by Pangsha. In The Pangsha Letters (Mills, 1995), Mills records how he travelled to the village with an armed escort to demand the return of heads that had been taken from another village. He also remarks that the Pitt Rivers Museum would "get some fine specimens" (see The Pitt Rivers Museum: A World Within, O'Hanlon, 2014: 114).This episode deserves particular attention because it reveals the complex relationship between colonial administration, military power, and the collection of human remains. Although Mills describes the expedition as an effort to protect neighbouring villages, his arrival with an armed escort and his demand for the heads must also be understood within the unequal power relations of the colonial administration. Mills's reference to the Museum receiving "fine specimens" is particularly revealing. It illustrates how human remains could be viewed as valuable additions to institutional collections, even when their acquisition was embedded in unequal colonial relationships. Such accounts invite us to reconsider the circumstances under which these remains were removed from their communities and transported to institutions thousands of miles away. The Scale of the Naga CollectionThe Museum's wider Naga collection comprises several thousand objects. Within it, 219 items are listed as Naga human-remains-related material: 39 ancestral human remains, primarily skulls, and 178 objects containing, or potentially containing, human hair. These figures underline the scale and complexity of the collection and the importance of engaging in its history. They also demonstrate why repatriation requires careful collaboration, historical research, and meaningful consultation with the communities concerned. Repatriation: Restoring Ancestral ConnectionsThe ongoing collaboration between the Pitt Rivers Museum, the Forum for Naga Reconciliation, and Naga communities across the homeland represents an important step towards addressing this history. Repatriation challenges the assumption that museums are necessarily the appropriate custodians of all the human remains and cultural materials they hold. It also raises important questions about the historical circumstances in which collections were assembled and the responsibilities of institutions towards the communities from whom these materials originated. For the Nagas, the return of their ancestors is deeply connected to questions of identity, belonging, memory, and dignity. These are not simply remains preserved for academic study; they are part of living histories and relationships that colonial collecting practices often failed to recognise. Ultimately, bringing the ancestors home is an act of historical recognition and human dignity. It is also a reminder that the work of decolonisation must extend beyond removing human remains from museum displays. It must involve listening to communities, acknowledging historical injustices, and enabling people to reclaim their relationships with their ancestors and their past. It is difficult to comprehend as to why the colonial powers betrayed the Nagas despite their sacrifices in both the World Wars; in France and in the Battle of Kohima. The remains were collected and taken away by the administrators who were themselves the guardians of the district - for a museum. So why shouldn’t the British Government take responsibility and tender an apology for such grave lapses during the Colonial Rule, and the Government of India should insist on return of all artefacts taken away from Nagaland. Acknowledgement:- Inputs have been obtained from the Website of Pitt Rivers Museum, Nagaland Gazette and Wikipediain compiling the above article.‘Ancestors are like stars in the night sky: we can’t always see them, but we know they’re always there.’ - Unknown

articles.title: Budgam meat seizure: FDA directs Railways to ensure licensed FBOs transport perishable food commodities under prescribed conditions
articles.description: Srinagar, Nov 19: The Food and Drugs Administration (FDA), Jammu and Kashmir, has issued an advisory to railway authorities, directing that highly perishable food commodities be transported only through duly licensed Food Business Operators (FBOs) and under prescribed temperature-controlled conditions, with proper declarations and documentation. The advisory follows the seizure and destruction of around 1,600 kg of frozen meat at Budgam Railway Station, where the consignment was allegedly transported through the railway parcel service by misrepresenting it as general goods. In a press statement, the FDA said the action was taken after receiving specific information from Railway Police authorities. The frozen meat was found to have been transported without proper temperature-control arrangements to maintain the required frozen conditions. A preliminary investigation revealed that the consignment originated from M/s Al Nida Foods, Ghazipur, Delhi, and was intended for Ayaan Manzoor, a resident of Bemina, Srinagar, through M/s Tultrav Courier Agency, Bemina. The consignment had reportedly been booked under the general parcel category without disclosing the actual nature of the commodity, apparently to circumvent the prescribed requirements for transporting highly perishable food products under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The FDA said inspection of the consignment and accompanying documents revealed discrepancies in the description of the commodity and violations of labelling norms, attracting provisions of Sections 53 and 61 of the Act. It was also found that the transporter and intended recipient did not possess the mandatory FSSAI licences, attracting penal provisions under Section 63. Considering the potential threat to public health, the entire consignment was seized and destroyed through the Municipal Committee, Budgam, at a designated disposal site. The department said notices had been issued to the concerned persons and entities, while further legal proceedings were being initiated under the relevant provisions of the Act. The FDA also referred to similar enforcement actions undertaken during 2025, when frozen meat and meat products were seized from five establishments across Srinagar. These included 1,200 kg from M/s Sunshine Industries, Zakura; 500 kg from M/s Al-Taqwa, Lasjan; 1,400 kg from M/s M.M. Foods, Haji Bagh, HMT; 420 kg from M/s Niyaz Ahmad Kawa, Aali Kadal; and 520 kg from M/s Al-Azeem Enterprises, Manderbagh. Following these seizures, legal proceedings were initiated against the respective Food Business Operators. The Court of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar, acting as the Adjudicating Officer, imposed penalties of Rs 4 lakh, Rs 5 lakh, Rs 4.40 lakh, Rs 1.25 lakh and Rs 17,500, respectively. The department further stated that two samples collected from the establishments were examined by the ICAR-National Meat Research Institute, Hyderabad, and identified as buffalo meat. To prevent such violations, the FDA had issued a prohibitory order on October 3, 2025, restricting the transportation, storage and sale of frozen food products without prescribed temperature-control arrangements and mandatory labelling under the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020. Meanwhile, the department said it had conducted 12,778 inspections across Jammu and Kashmir during the financial year 2026-27, lifting 7,266 enforcement samples and 2,857 surveillance samples for analysis through NABL-accredited laboratories. During the same period, 533 cases were instituted and 619 cases adjudicated, resulting in penalties amounting to Rs 1,00,42,231 under various provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act. Following the Budgam incident, FDA field teams intensified enforcement activities, conducting 364 inspections, suspending nine FSSAI licences or registrations, issuing 21 improvement notices and recommending 31 cases for adjudication. More than 19 cases were also compounded under Section 69 of the Act. The FDA also said that funding-related issues concerning manpower and laboratory requirements had been resolved after the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), Government of India, approved the action plan submitted by the department for the financial years 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29. The approval will facilitate the recruitment of laboratory analysts, microbiologists, drivers and other personnel, besides procurement of chemicals, consumables and glassware for the government food laboratories in Srinagar and Jammu. The procurement process for laboratory manpower through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal has reached its final stage, while the procurement of certified reference materials, chemicals and glassware is expected to be completed within two weeks, the department said. Annual maintenance contracts for high-end laboratory equipment have also been executed with the respective original equipment manufacturers, while method validation is underway. Contracts for hiring drivers and laboratory analysts for Mobile Food Testing Vans have also been finalised, with personnel being deployed for operational activities. The department said it was working to expand the NABL-accredited testing scope of the government food laboratories to 2,500 parameters by January 2027 and 3,500 parameters by March 2027. Additional NABL-accredited and FSSAI-recognised laboratories are also being empanelled to strengthen testing capacity and ensure timely analysis of enforcement and surveillance samples. The FDA said it would continue intensified surveillance and enforcement to ensure compliance with food safety standards and appealed to consumers to share specific information about violations with the department for timely action.

articles.title: MSME Ministry Showcases Traditional Industries and Manufacturing Innovations at IITF 2026
articles.description: MSME Ministry Showcases Traditional Industries and Manufacturing Innovations at IITF 2026 New Delhi, Nov 19 (KNN) Union Minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Jitan Ram Manjhi inaugurated the Ministry of MSME, Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board and National SC-ST Hub (NSSH) pavilions at the 45th India International Trade Fair (IITF) at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on Wednesday. Minister of State for MSME Shobha Karandlaje was also present. The pavilions, themed ‘MSME-Vikas Bhi, Virasat Bhi’, showcase India's traditional industries, manufacturing capabilities and entrepreneurial ecosystem. MSME Sector Generates 42 Crore Jobs Addressing the media, Manjhi highlighted the role of MSMEs in generating employment, particularly for India's youth. He said, "Registration of MSMEs has now crossed 10 crore, generating employment to 42 crore persons." He also noted that the Udyam Assist Portal was simplifying registration for micro enterprises and that the pavilion aimed to encourage young people to take up entrepreneurship. Following the inauguration, Manjhi and Karandlaje visited the stalls and witnessed demonstrations of traditional manufacturing processes. MSME Secretary Bharat Khera and Additional Secretary and Development Commissioner Rajneesh were also present. MSME Pavilion Features 437 Stalls The MSME Pavilion features 437 stalls, including 292 MSME units, 101 KVIC participants, 34 NSSH enterprises and 10 coir-sector participants. More than 98 percent of the participating MSMEs are first-time exhibitors. Entrepreneurs from 29 States and Union Territories are participating. Women account for 57.87 percent of participants, while SC/ST entrepreneurs represent 27.73 percent. Persons with disabilities and 15 PM Vishwakarma beneficiaries are also showcasing their products. Exhibits include textiles, handlooms, handicrafts, green products, ceramics, metal crafts, leather goods, toys and regional products. Technology displays featuring drones and Chandrayaan components developed with MSME participation are also on display. Coir Pavilion Showcases Research and Innovation The Coir Board Pavilion brings together research institutions, artisan groups and small-scale manufacturers to showcase technological developments and new applications in the coir sector. Key exhibits include coir geotextiles, vertical gardens, biodegradable products, coir wood, soilless cultivation, coir net houses and coir pith composting. A portable coir-based lawn, called CocoLoawn, is another attraction. NSSH Supports SC/ST Enterprises Under the National SC-ST Hub scheme, 34 SC/ST micro and small enterprises from seven states have been provided dedicated stalls to showcase their products and connect with institutional and bulk buyers. The initiative also supports the government's 4 percent public procurement target from SC/ST-owned MSEs, while helping participating businesses improve brand visibility, establish business contacts and explore new markets. Khadi Pavilion Highlights Traditional Manufacturing The Khadi India Pavilion features 101 stalls showcasing products made by artisans from different regions. A dedicated studio for the ‘Khadi Ki Baat’ podcast has also been set up to promote awareness of Khadi through conversations with artisans and industry stakeholders. Live demonstrations include traditional and electric charkhas, handloom weaving, pottery, oil extraction using the traditional kolhu (ghani), and the making of soap, honey products, leather footwear, incense sticks and dhoop. (KNN Bureau)
